This stage asks why every moving thing needs a mover, and whether the chain of movers can continue without end. It examines God's power and the powers of the soul, how the soul differs from the body's physical condition, and why beings free of matter neither die nor seek anything through motion. It then considers what things are made from, why they begin after not existing, and whether the possibility of coming to be is an added feature. It examines possibility and actuality, and the different ways power and action can come before one another. Finally, it looks at how nature and substances change, how bodies, the world, beings free of matter, and time come into existence, what causes time and what it belongs to, and why nothing comes before time except God.

The word power is used for several different things, but its earliest meaning seems to be the strength an animal has to carry out strenuous movements. Its opposite is weakness. In this sense, power is a kind of added strength in the ability to act. It has a source and a sign. Its source is the ability to act: an animal acts when it wills and does not act when it does not will. The opposite of this ability is inability. Its sign is resistance to being affected. Someone carrying out strenuous movements may be affected by the effort, and that can keep them from finishing what they are doing. So resistance to being affected points to strength. The word power then came to be used both for its source—the ability to act—and for its sign—the ability to resist being affected.

Power also has a general description and a feature that follows from it. Its general description is a quality that affects something else, considered as something distinct from itself. The feature that follows is possibility. Someone with power can act, but can also refrain from acting, so whether the action occurs remains open. Since possibility follows from power in this sense, the word power also came to mean possibility itself. That is why people say a white garment is “black potentially”: it can become black.

People also call attainment and existence “act,” even when, strictly speaking, these are not actions but states that are received. The original meaning of power was tied to action. So once people called possibility “power,” they called what that possibility leads to—attainment and existence—“act.”

Mathematicians noticed that some lines can serve as a side of a particular square, while others cannot. They called the square the “power” of the line, as though the square were something that could potentially come from it. Some held that the square is formed when one of its sides turns around itself.

Once we understand power, we can identify its opposites: weakness, inability, ease of being affected, necessity, ineffectiveness, and a line's inability to serve as a side of a given square. Each is opposed to power in a different respect. We have already discussed possibility as one meaning of power. But possibility opposed to actuality differs in one respect from possibility opposed to necessary existence or impossibility. This will become clear when we discuss why matter is needed for everything that comes to be or changes. Power as resistance to being affected is one kind of quality. Power as strength or ability seems to be a kind of active quality—a quality that produces an effect.
II. Defining power as the source of change

Power can mean the source of change in one thing that brings about change in another, insofar as the other is distinct from it. We add that last qualification because if something acted on itself—as when a doctor treats himself—it would have to differ from itself in some respect or have different parts. Otherwise, the same thing would be both the one acting and the one affected in the very same respect. That is impossible, even for something made of parts, let alone something simple.

A feature may follow necessarily from what a thing is, without the thing first having to become able to receive it. This is the exception: the feature is already fully present, as with features that necessarily belong to what a thing is. Some writers, including the author of Al-Mulakhkhas, saw that something can seem to act and be acted on in this different sense. They then began to doubt that one thing cannot be both agent and recipient. But the difference between what is possible and what is actual is clear and certain.

There is no doubt that nothing can be the source of its own change. If a thing were the source of a feature or state in itself, that feature would remain for as long as the thing did. The thing would not be changing. So the source of its change must be something else. This shows that every moving thing has a mover other than itself.

An agent's power may involve awareness and choice, or it may involve neither. Each kind can be divided further. The capacity to be affected may belong to bodies or to souls. A thing may be able to take on a form without keeping it, as water takes the shape of a container but does not hold that shape. Or it may be able both to take on a form and keep it, as wax and earth do.

An affected thing may be able to undergo one kind of change, like a heavenly sphere's rotation; a limited range of changes, like an animal; or any change at all, like basic matter. An agent's power may likewise be limited to one action, like fire's power to burn; it may extend to many but limited actions, as with the choices of those who can choose; or it may extend to everything, as God's power does: He has power over all things.

Here is a rule that applies to both kinds of power: the more fully formed a thing is, the more it can act and the less it is acted upon. The less fully formed it is, the more it is acted upon and the less it acts. God—may His name be exalted—has the fullest and strongest existence. He acts on all things and is the goal toward which all things tend. His power extends without limit. Basic matter, by contrast, is as indeterminate as anything can be. It is like the broadest class of things because it is bare of every form that would make things distinct kinds and give them actual existence. It can receive all things, as the broadest class can include every kind. I do not mean that basic matter is ready for every form at once. Readiness is a specific capacity for one change that is close to taking place, and it arises only through a specific form. Basic matter is not, by itself, ready for every form; a particular form makes it ready for a particular thing.
Let us now divide powers by the actions they produce. A power may produce one action or several. In either case, it may act with awareness or without it. This gives us four kinds.

The first kind is a power that produces one action without awareness of that action. It may be a form that makes a thing what it is, or a feature that does not. In things such as fire and water it is called a nature. In bodies made from different elements, it is called the form of that kind of body; examples include opium's cooling nature and euphorbium's heating nature. If it is a feature of the second kind, examples include heat and cold.

These are the four kinds of power. They cannot all be grouped under one general type, because some are forms that make a thing what it is, while others are features a thing can have. We discuss the first kind when we study matter and form, the second and third when we study the soul, and the fourth when we study qualities.

One more point should be clear. A power to act may be limited to one action, like fire's power to burn, or may extend to several actions, like the power of someone who can choose what to do. When a power can act on any one of many possible individuals of a kind, outside causes determine which particular individual it acts on. Once that individual exists, the power with respect to that specific individual is gone. If it remained, the same result would be both actual and still only possible. But the power to act on another individual of the same kind does not disappear. The power to act on any individual of that kind remains even when no action is taking place.

It is like the difference between a general idea and an idea tied to one particular person. A general idea does not disappear when one person is gone. But an idea tied to one person in particular ends when that person is gone. As we have explained, necessity stands to possibility as completeness stands to lack. So possibility does not disappear when it becomes necessary, but the power to perform one specific action does disappear once that action is complete.
III. Must the ability to act exist when the action happens?
Some thinkers held that the ability to act must exist at the same time as the action. Avicenna rejected this as implausible. In the metaphysics section of The Healing, he says:

On this view, a person sitting down cannot be able to stand. The ability would come only once the person was already standing—so how could they stand? Such a person would also be unable to see or look around several times in a single day. In effect, they would be blind.
It is even more surprising that the author of Al-Mulakhkhas tries to defend their view this way:

The objection Avicenna raises does not seem justified. If you define power as the source of change, then either all the conditions needed for it to bring about an effect are present, or they are not. If they are all present, the effect must occur at the same time as the power; the power cannot come before the effect. In that sense, we can say the power and action happen together. But if a condition needed to produce the effect is missing, what is present is not the full cause, but only part of it. It is not the full power to act, but only part of that power. The quality called ability clearly exists both before and after the action. But it is not the full power to produce the action; it is only one part. If we can understand their words this way, why accuse them of error and make their view look foolish?

I say that this defender has confused two meanings of power. One is the ability to act while the action is still only possible. The other is the full power that produces the action once all its conditions are in place. He also seems to have forgotten that he already admitted possibility follows from the first kind of power. He did not see that this possibility is only readiness for an action, not the action itself. It cannot exist together with the completed action. This differs from the way the mind considers what something is apart from whether it exists. The mind can make that distinction even for simple things that do exist in reality.

The word source also has two meanings. It can mean what makes something possible, or what makes it actual. The form present in semen is a source of the possibility of a human being, but it cannot by itself bring an actual human being into existence. Otherwise, power as power would already be actual in relation to the very thing it is only able to bring about. Yet the defender also admits that an incomplete cause cannot produce its effect; once complete, it must produce it. A thing cannot be incomplete and complete, or impossible and necessary, in the same respect.

What makes both action and inaction possible cannot, without anything more, be the source of one particular action. The source of ability—the possibility of acting—is one thing. The source that makes the action real and necessary is another. How can anyone, by reason and common sense, claim that the ability to do something exists only when the action is happening? If we think carefully about what we mean by a source of change, we see that, in relation to the change it can bring about, the result must still be possible and not yet real. A source of something that follows from it necessarily should not be called the source of change in another thing. I will make this clearer.
IV. When must a change happen, and when can it fail to happen?

When a limited power to act meets a limited capacity to be affected, the action must follow. Power to act is also called ability. If it involves awareness and choice, it is an ability whether or not the action always follows without fail.

Theologians say that ability belongs only to someone who can both act and refrain from acting. So they do not call a cause that always acts a capable agent, even if it is fully able to do so. This view is wrong. It is right only if “capable” means that both acting and refraining are possible, and neither is settled on its own. Animal ability works this way: it needs something to tip the balance, such as a motive, before it can act. But if we define a capable agent as one whose action comes with awareness and will, then anyone who acts by will is capable and free. The statement “if it wills, it acts; if it does not will, it does not act” is true whether not willing can actually happen or is impossible. A conditional statement like this does not depend on either part being true on its own, and does not require an alternative to occur. There are several kinds of capable agent.

One kind is an agent that acts by intention. In itself, it is equally related to two possible outcomes, so it needs something extra to tip the balance. That might be new knowledge, or the presence of something to act on and its readiness to receive the action. A writer, for example, needs a tablet with a smooth surface. The agent may need a tool, such as a pen or a chisel; a helper, as one sawyer needs another; a suitable time, as a leatherworker needs summer; or a motive, as hunger prompts someone to eat. It may also need an obstacle removed: a dyer needs dirt cleared from the cloth, and a washer needs the clouds to pass so the cloth can dry.

A motive is different from will. An agent acting by will may have an additional motive, or may have none. A motive may also arise after being absent. In all these cases, the agent is still described as acting by will.

Another kind is an agent whose action comes from its knowledge. Its knowledge of the order and goodness of the action is the only source and motive for acting; nothing is added to the knowledge itself. This is how the Necessary Being acts, according to the philosophers in Aristotle’s school.

A third kind is an agent whose own self-knowledge is enough to bring about its action. Its knowledge of what it makes is identical with the being of what it makes, just as its knowledge of itself as maker is identical with itself. This is how God acts, according to the Illuminationist philosophers, who regard Him as light. His light—His knowledge of Himself—is what makes other beings appear in the world. His first creations are the ruling and guiding lights of intellect and soul. Through them come lesser lights and beings with awareness, some constant and some passing, down through all existence from the brightest to the darkest.

These three kinds all act by choice and will, guided by knowledge. The knowledge may be separate from the agent, be an added feature that always belongs to it, or be identical with it. Every other kind of agent acts under compulsion, and there are three such kinds.

One kind acts by nature. It acts according to its bodily nature when nothing blocks it. A second kind acts under force: its nature is made to act against its usual direction by an outside force. If left alone, it would act otherwise. A third kind acts under the direction of a higher power. This happens when a stronger power guides a natural power and uses it to produce movements and changes in the body below. For example, the powers of plants and animals serve the soul by drawing things in, pushing them out, changing them, digesting food, growing, and reproducing. These actions are neither simply the body's nature acting on its own, nor actions against its nature. They follow the higher principles that guide these powers and help make them what they are. This kind of action differs from natural action, forced action, and voluntary action as such.

For example, when the soul moves the body by choice, the movement belongs both to the soul and to the body. In relation to the soul, we call it voluntary. In relation to the body or one of its parts, we call it action under direction.

All three kinds are compelled in some way. If we look closely, only God acts by choice in the fullest sense. All others act under His power, whether they choose or are forced. Many are compelled even in their very act of choosing.

Returning to our question, some powers that start movements and actions work with reason and imagination, while others do not. The powers linked to reason and imagination do not act on their own just because something is present for them to act on. Nor does the meeting of a power with something that can be affected make the action inevitable. Just as bodily matter can be equally ready for two opposite forms, these mental powers can be equally ready for opposite possibilities when considered on their own. One power of the intellect can take in both human and nonhuman things; one power in an animal can imagine both pleasure and pain, a thing and its opposite.

In themselves, these powers can act in either direction. They become able to bring about an action only when joined by a will that grows from belief or thought, or by a desire raised by imagining something pleasant or painful. In short, there must be a motive that gives rise to a firm resolve, one that does not turn away from its aim. This resolve moves the nerves and muscles, and then the action becomes necessary. If these powers alone forced action whenever they were present, they would produce two opposing actions at once, which is impossible.

Powers in beings without reason and imagination may also be able to act without always doing so. But their action becomes necessary when the power is complete, every obstacle is removed, and it meets a capacity to be affected. Likewise, a capacity to be affected must undergo change when it meets a power to act only if that capacity is complete. Like a power to act, it may be complete or incomplete. An incomplete capacity is far from producing the change; a complete one is close. There are different degrees of distance.

Semen has the potential to become a man, and so does a boy. But the potential in semen is more remote: it must meet two powers to act, one that brings it to childhood and another that develops the child into an adult man. A boy needs to meet only one such power to reach adulthood. More remote still is the capacity in an element, and farther away than that is basic matter's capacity to become an intellect fully at work—even an intellect able to understand ideas below it, as we will explain later.
V. Another way to divide the power to act

Power to act may be a source of existence or a source of change. Philosophers who study existence and its causes call an agent the source that gives existence. Those who study nature mean the source of change, in its different forms. The first is more deserving of the name “agent.” A source of change is itself subject to change: it renews a state that was different before. It is like a changing tool. It moves and is moved, acts and is acted upon, and is kept in being while also changing and passing away.

If you ask who most deserves the name “agent,” the answer is God. He removes nonexistence completely from things and removes their deficiency and evil. His action is the unbounded giving of good and existence. It is not limited to a period, conditioned by a quality, or confined to one time rather than another. It is eternal and necessary, in measure with what each recipient can bear and each prepared thing can receive.

The powers that directly cause movement do something else. They prepare matter and make it ready. They remove some opposing qualities so matter can receive another form once those qualities are gone, or divide it according to its different levels of readiness. They do not give existence itself.
VI. Another way to divide causes

When we discuss causes and effects, you will see how something can be a cause only indirectly. Keep this in mind here: most things people call agents do not truly give existence to the things attributed to them. A father, a farmer, or a builder, for example, does not give existence to children, crops, or buildings. They prepare the conditions that allow these things to come about, so they are only indirect causes. God is the one who gives them existence. He points this out when He says:

Have you considered the seed you emit? Do you create it, or are We the Creator? Have you considered what you sow? Do you make it grow, or are We the One who makes it grow? Have you considered the fire you kindle? Did you make its tree grow, or are We the One who made it grow?
The point is that what most people call an agent only sets things in motion and brings about changes in matter. God is the one who gives things their forms and existence. Exalted is His name.
VII. Another way to classify abilities to act

Some abilities to act come from nature, some from habit, some from learned skill, and some from chance. To learn a skill, a person deliberately uses materials, tools, and movements. With practice, the soul gains a lasting ability that lets the action come easily. This ability gives the skill its character, much as fire's nature makes it heat and water's nature makes it cool. In our discussion of the next life, we will see that this lasting ability may become part of what the soul is, and that the soul may be raised in that form on the Day of Resurrection.

Actions done from habit, on the other hand, may start for another reason—desire, anger, or an opinion. Habit then develops as a result; the person did not set out to form it or direct their actions toward it from the start. A habit does not have to mean that the same actions have taken root in the soul. Repeating them may create something else in the soul, something different from the actions themselves. The actions prepare the soul for it, and what prepares something need not be like what it prepares. So a skill learned through practice differs from a habit that grows out of repeated action.

A habit does not have to depend on particular tools or materials. The habit of walking, for example, is very different from the habit of trading. Even so, if we look closely, we see that habits and learned skills both grow from the same basic quality in the soul. Natural abilities are found in both nonliving and living bodies. We will explain chance, randomness, and aimless action when we discuss what things are for.
VIII. Does every action have to start after a time when it did not exist?

Not every action has to come after a time when it did not exist, as the theologians claim. They hold that something needs a cause because it began to exist, not simply because it is possible. The only exception would be if they use “action” to mean a particular kind of effect that happens while an agent acts on something—for example, heating an object while it is being heated, or darkening it while it is being darkened. But if “an agent’s action” means giving something existence, it does not have to come after a time when it did not exist. An effect needs a cause because it is possible, not because it once did not exist.

Some actions are renewed moment by moment, such as motion and time, and nature as it works through bodies. They need a cause to begin, but not to keep existing, since they do not last from one moment to the next. They also need a cause because they are possible: they come into being and change. We will explain this later.
But the theologians do not mean this. They even say that if God ceased to exist after bringing the world into being, the world would still exist.

Those who have examined this carefully say that a caused thing cannot exist on its own. Its existence depends on the cause that brings it into being and keeps it in being. This dependence does not come from what the thing is, because the cause did not make its nature. It does not come from the time before it existed, because the cause did not make it nonexistent. Nor does it come simply from the fact that it came after not existing. That order is part of the kind of existence it has; it does not need a cause of its own.

Instead, a new thing depends on its cause because its existence cannot stand on its own. It is too weak and incomplete to be whole without something else. Its cause completes it. Dependence ends with God, whose own reality is complete. Through Him, all that is complete is completed, every need is met, and every movement and longing reaches its goal. This prevents the explanation from looping back on itself or going on forever. God is fully complete and more than complete, as we have explained. Everything else depends on Him and needs Him. As we have said, this dependence is part of what holds everything else up.

If things coming into being were fully ready to receive existence, they would always exist. But they become ready through changes that happen one after another. These changes complete their ability to exist. Once that ability is complete, they exist without delay. So an action happens as soon as its cause is fully in place. This is why Aristotle said that an action that happens in time must come from a cause that also exists in time. He explains:
To find out whether the cause of an action exists in time, look at the action itself. If it takes place in time, so does its cause, because the cause cannot be separated from it.
IX. Power is not the body's temperament, as some doctors claim

Here is why. As we will explain, bodily temperament is a blend of the basic qualities we feel by touch: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. It is a mix of these four, balanced among them and weaker than each one on its own. Its effects should therefore be like theirs, but weaker. Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness have direct, strong effects; the body's blended temperament has mild, weak effects.

Since the soul's power does not have the same kind of effect as these four qualities, it cannot be the temperament itself. Instead, power is a quality of the soul that depends on the body's temperament. It, in turn, calls for a guiding form that manages and preserves that temperament. This form replaces, little by little, what the body loses as it changes, and repairs what tends to come apart under the opposing effects and shifting conditions of those qualities. So this guiding form, with its ability to direct, repair, and control, belongs to a higher level than the body's temperament. This question fits better in the study of nature.

Motion and rest resemble potentiality and actuality. In the broadest sense, they are features of things simply insofar as they exist; a thing need not first be classified as a particular natural or mathematical kind for them to apply. An existing thing is either actual in every respect, so that it cannot change or leave its state; potential in every respect, though this can apply to something that exists only when its potentiality itself has some actuality, as it does in prime matter; or actual in one respect and potential in another. In the last case, it must be made up of two aspects: one actual, the other potential. As actual, it comes before what is potential in it. We will see that actuality comes before potentiality in every sense of “before.”

The first kind—what is actual in every respect and cannot change at all—must be truly simple. Yet, despite its simplicity, it must contain all things and the fullness of all existence, as we will prove. A thing that is actual in one respect and potential in another must be brought from potentiality to actuality by something other than itself, in the respect in which it is potential. Otherwise, it would not be potential.

This transition can happen gradually or all at once. In the broad sense, transition from potentiality to actuality occurs in every category: in each one, something can move from potential to actual. But the established use of the word motion is narrower. It means a transition that does not happen all at once. The absence of such a transition in something capable of receiving it is called rest. Motion can therefore be defined as gradual coming-to-be, gradual arrival, or a step-by-step transition from potentiality to actuality. Each of these phrases can define motion.

You might object that “all at once” means coming to be in an instant; an instant is the boundary of time; and time is the measure of motion. So defining motion by what happens all at once seems to define it through time, which is itself defined through motion. That would make the definition circular. The same problem seems to arise if we say “step by step” or “gradually,” since both are understood through time, which is understood through motion.

We can answer, as some careful thinkers have, that we grasp these ideas—happening all at once, happening gradually, and the like—directly, with help from the senses. Defining them precisely may require their essential parts, such as time and the instant. Those precise definitions, however, are what need proof. We can define motion using these familiar ideas, then use motion to understand time and the instant: one is its measure, the other the boundary of that measure. Time and the instant are what account for these ideas that we grasp at once. Many things are immediately familiar to us even though their true nature is hard to explain. There is no circle here. This answer was given by the author of Discussions and approved by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Eastern Investigations. Earlier philosophers, however, rejected this definition because they thought it contained a hidden circle.

For a gradual process to count, though, it must be laid out along something extended that comes to be gradually. That is why Avicenna says in The Healing that all such definitions involve circular reasoning. Our master in this discipline therefore took another path. Earlier philosophers set these definitions aside and said that motion is a potential arrival. Whatever a thing can arrive at is a completion for that thing. Motion, then, is a completion of what moves. But it differs from other kinds of completion: its whole nature lies in passing toward something else and moving along the way to it. This gives it two features. First, there must be some attainable goal toward which the movement is directed. Second, as long as the movement is still under way, something about it remains potential. A thing is moving in actuality only while it has not reached its goal. Until then, some part of the goal remains potential for it. Motion therefore depends on some part of it remaining potential, and on the goal not yet being fully actual. Other completions have neither feature. When something that is potentially square becomes square, its squareness does not require it to keep reaching for anything. And once the square shape is present, no part of it remains potential.

Consider a body in one place that could be in another. It has two possibilities: being in that other place, and moving toward it. We have already seen that whatever a thing could attain would be a completion for it. So moving toward the goal is a completion. But it must come before reaching the goal; otherwise, there would be no gradual arrival, which is what we are discussing. Thus, moving toward the goal is the first completion of what is potential. It is not a completion of the body in every respect. Motion does not complete the body simply as a body; it completes it in the respect in which it was potential. Motion, then, is the first completion of what is potential, precisely insofar as it is potential. This is the definition given by Aristotle, the greatest philosopher.

Plato, the divine philosopher, defined motion as “leaving equality”: a thing’s state at one instant is no longer the same as it was just before or just after. Pythagoras is reported to have defined motion as “otherness.” This comes close to Plato’s definition: at every instant, the thing differs in some respect from how it was just before and how it will be just after. We can make both definitions more complete by understanding them to include continuous gradual change. If a thing’s state at each moment differs from its state at another moment before or after, then its successive states are different, yet form one continuous process. Plato called this “leaving equality”; Pythagoras called it “otherness.” They mean much the same thing.

It would be no objection that “leaving equality” and “otherness” are each simple ideas and do not, by themselves, express extension and continuity. The point is that the definitions can be understood in the fuller sense just described. Avicenna did not take this approach. In The Healing, he says that motion has been defined in several confused ways because its nature is itself hard to grasp. Its stages are never fixed in actuality: as one state passes away, another begins. Some defined it as “otherness,” since motion changes a state and brings about something different from what was there before. But they failed to see that what brings about otherness need not itself be otherness. Not everything that produces something is identical with what it produces. If otherness itself were motion, then everything different would be moving, which is not so.

Some have called motion an unlimited nature. At most, Avicenna says, this could be one of its features, and not a feature unique to motion; infinity and time are unlimited in the same way. Others defined it as “leaving equality”: a stable state is one that remains the same in relation to every passing time, while in motion the relation between the thing and its states is not the same at different times. A body moving from place to place is in a different place at every instant; something changing in quality has a different quality at every instant. These definitions were attempts to cope with a difficult subject. We do not need to spend a long time rejecting them; a sound mind can see the problem from what we have already said. That is the end of Avicenna’s account.

I say: Avicenna’s criticism of the Pythagorean definition does not quite hold. Motion is not something that causes otherness; motion is change itself, a thing’s passing from one state to another. It is not whatever makes the thing change. A thing’s leaving one state is itself its being different from that state in reality, even if the two ideas differ in our minds. That is enough for a definition. As for the definition attributed to some thinkers—that motion is an unlimited nature—we will discuss it when we prove that the substance of nature is constantly changing and flowing through every body. This constant renewal in nature’s own substance is the source of all the changing motions and qualities of earthly things.

In Eastern Investigations and his commentary on The Sources of Wisdom, Fakhr al-Din al-Razi raises a doubt about the claim that a thing comes from potentiality to actuality gradually, although the philosophers agree on it. When something changes, he says, either something comes to be in it or something leaves it. If neither happens—if nothing absent appears and nothing present disappears—then its state at that instant is the same as before, so it has not changed. But change was assumed. Therefore, when a thing changes, something must come to be in it or leave it.

Suppose something comes to be in it. That thing was absent and then became present, so it must have a beginning. The beginning cannot be divided, or one part would come before the other and would not be the beginning itself. At its beginning, then, the new thing either exists or does not. If it does not exist, it is still absent and has not begun to exist. If it does exist, then either some part of it remains potential or none does. If none remains, the whole thing came to be at once, not gradually. If some part remains potential, that remaining part is either the very same thing that has come to be—which is impossible, since one thing cannot be present and absent at once—or it is something else. In the latter case, what came first came to be all at once, while what has not yet come to be is wholly absent. No one thing has come to be gradually; there are only separate things following one another. The conclusion, al-Razi says, is that a simple, indivisible thing can only come to be all at once. A thing with many parts can be said to come to be gradually only because each part appears after another. Strictly speaking, anything that has come to be has come to be all at once, and whatever has not come to be is wholly absent. That is his argument.

I reply that Bahmanyar records this objection from earlier philosophers and rejects it. It only denies motion as a continuous whole, he says, which does not exist in external things. What exists is motion as “being between” its endpoints: a flowing state, neither something that has yet to begin nor something that has already come to an end. Most later philosophers took this approach, claiming it was the right philosophical view. But our master and teacher—may his standing remain high—explained that even those who deny motion as a continuous whole still imagine this “being between” as a new, gradually unfolding, continuous thing, whose parts arise one after another. If one thing cannot come to be gradually, how can we imagine it doing so, whether in the external world or in the mind? This misleading argument would prove just as much about imagined things as about external ones, even though everyone agrees it fails. How, then, can it be sound here?
